extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, city/beat reporters, publicity writers, and city editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reporting local business news and for planning/writing publicity (public relations/propaganda) material for newspapers, including ethics, sourcing, translation of financial jargon, and step-by-step rules for running publicity campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping confidences makes or wrecks a reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reporter must guard promises of confidentiality rigorously; a reputation as a promise-breaker will ruin a reporter's career. Be extremely thorough in handling sources' trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify off-the-record source if information duplicated
rubrics_metrics.description: If one man gives information 'off the record' and another gives the same information for publication, tell the first man before the story appears so he won't think his promise was broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the same facts come from both confidential and on-the-record sources, proactively inform the off‑the‑record source prior to publication to preserve trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write business stories in plain English
rubrics_metrics.description: WRITE THEM IN ENGLISH — translate business/financial phrasing into language ordinary readers understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: convert terse, technical statements (e.g., cumulative preferred dividend arrears) into clear, explanatory paragraphs so non‑specialist readers can follow; generous explanations justify extra wordage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write business news for general readers, not specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Business news written for specialist readers is too expensive; written for the generality of readers, it is worth while.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clarity and explanation to expand readership rather than dense specialist language that alienates most readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Chamber of Commerce as an early tip-off source
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chamber of Commerce is the repository of local business statistics and an excellent tip‑off station for certain kinds of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. of C. often has early access to data (e.g., local payroll figures) and will report small advances in community prosperity; use it for leads and early figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Chamber of Commerce statements skeptically
rubrics_metrics.description: About unfavorable news the Chamber is sphinxlike or may 'talk with a forked tongue' — because it tends to spin bad developments favorably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that C. of C. viewpoints can be advocacy; present their claims as argument/propaganda and verify before treating them as facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely solely on a Chamber executive; seek committee and other sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid assuming the Executive Director is the only news source in the Chamber; committee members constitute a collective source of high importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look beyond the official spokesperson to merchants and committee members for information and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember small businesses as news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't ignore the 'little fellow' — small firms and shops often have newsworthy reputations, specialized skills, or gossip that leads to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate small manufacturers and merchants (e.g., firms with unique products or processes) and use local gossip as a starting point for verification and further reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t presume inside tracks always available; executives may guard processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives hesitate to describe new processes partly for patent concerns and competitor secrecy, but sometimes they will explain innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to proprietary concerns but persistent in asking 'How was it done?' — you may obtain usable explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt metropolitan reporting tips to local angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Metropolitan papers give tips that local reporters can adapt to local stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broader/regulatory news (e.g., ICC rate changes) as a springboard to ask local businesses how such changes will affect them, producing locally relevant paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish advertising from news
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter should be able to distinguish between advertising and news; news need not be bad to be free of advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just because a business's name appears in news doesn't mean it's advertising; remain alert to promotional intent and avoid publishing puffery as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trade and professional magazines for sideline pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Every occupation has trade journals; a reporter is well placed to contribute descriptive or how‑it‑was‑done pieces and can be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for descriptive features (e.g., inventive window displays) that interest trade publications; these can be legitimate side income if they don't conflict with reporting duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unauthorized publicity writing while reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining publicity with reporting means a divided loyalty; newspapers increasingly prohibit staff from writing publicity without permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized publicity work (especially commercial) risks diluted reporting and conflicts; get the city editor's consent before taking outside publicity assignments; civic/nonprofit roles are more likely to be permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that commercial publicity can force a choice of loyalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Working for commercial publicity (e.g., promoting weak fights) can pressure a reporter to embellish news and mislead readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assignments that require you to misstate or overhype events that you might later need to cover as a reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand three branches of publicity work
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity splits into: (1) space grafting, (2) propaganda, (3) public relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space grafting (peddling free ads) is unethical and fading; propaganda has acceptable and unacceptable forms; public relations (explaining genuine organizational activity) is the most valuable and honorable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid space grafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Space grafting is fading and unethical — every inch of stolen space diverts money from advertising and harms the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not practice or tolerate planting fake news solely to obtain free newspaper space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hidden/masked propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden propaganda conceals its source and presents arguments as if they were facts — this is patently undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and refuse material that hides its parentage; demand disclosure of source and sponsorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and label open, honest propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Open propaganda that discloses its source (e.g., a company president) is acceptable; readers can judge it as opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material is advocacy but openly attributed, it may be used — but it must be presented as opinion/argument, not fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as socially valuable publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining to a community what an organization or company does is socially valuable — genuine PR is news that newspapers otherwise might miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR material that conveys real developments (e.g., employment policy changes, technical breakthroughs) should be welcomed if factual and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity writer remains a reporter, not an advertising writer
rubrics_metrics.description: A publicity writer must follow journalistic standards: he is a reporter for his employer and should deliver genuine news, not advertising copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the 'whats' and 'whys' and document genuine developments rather than selling products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan publicity: prioritize timing and building to a climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning involves two central considerations: timing, and building to a climax — success hinges on these principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sustained, strategically timed sequence of stories is more effective than random, spontaneous releases; design the campaign arc in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: One person must be in command of a publicity campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: The publicity must be centralized under some one director who alone releases stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncoordinated volunteers each issuing copy; enforce that all stories follow the publicity director's strategy to prevent spoiling the campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and time campaign items so each story remains interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: A campaign must be spaced and timed so that each story is interesting; random dumping results in early sparkle followed by drab pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence items to sustain interest across the campaign; avoid clustering strong items together and leaving weak ones later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity stories must be news, not puffery
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write stories just to fill space — if there is no news, don't write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers can spot empty publicity; build reputation by bringing real stories rather than frequent fluff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each publicity story must present a new feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story must have a new feature; twice‑told publicity stories have no chance of getting in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each installment adds distinct information rather than repeating previous points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter campaigns are usually more effective
rubrics_metrics.description: The shorter a campaign, the better it is likely to be; a few lively stories beat many weak ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for focused bursts (e.g., a fortnight to three weeks) rather than protracted series of diminishing returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build the campaign to a climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan to attract interest early and induce readers to act at the end — close with a 'crackle'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve strong material for the closing so the campaign converts interest into action (ticket sales, donations, participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the campaign to city editors but do not solicit favors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell editors what the plan is and supply information, but don't ask them to give preferential treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present yourself as helpful and reasonable; the surprise of a non‑pleading approach often yields cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overlapping and repetitive tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Make each story brand‑new; overlapping tales lead editors to dismiss the material as repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate content to avoid presenting the same facts across successive pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be a space hog; prefer shorter stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Long column‑length pieces are harder to place and risk exhausting a paper's willingness to run your material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short stories where possible; they have higher chance of placement and lower 'mortality' rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide stories so morning and evening papers each get fresh news
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate or time items so both morning and evening editions receive new material rather than rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the sequence so each paper benefits from new angles, keeping news fresh for competing editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat competing papers scrupulously alike
rubrics_metrics.description: Give Record and Journal the same fairness in stories and pictures; don't favor one by always giving them the carbon copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either produce fresh stories for each paper or alternate carbons so no paper feels treated as secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid far‑ahead release dates on minor news
rubrics_metrics.description: Far‑ahead release dates (weeks ahead) for minor‑league news are foolish; a day or so is long enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre‑dating copy to appear important is ineffective for routine news and risks being filed away and forgotten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write factual publicity copy even when facts are hard to get
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity that is only words and no facts is doomed; editors prefer fewer substantial pieces over many thin ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather verifiable facts to back claims; the publicity writer's reputation rests on producing substantial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time stories for days when the paper is large and submit early
rubrics_metrics.description: Monday and Saturday are tight issues; best days are Thursday/Friday or Tuesday depending on advertising cycles. Submit early (by 3pm day before for morning papers, by 8am for afternoon editions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule delivery to coincide with the paper's capacity to print more features and ensure copy reaches the desk before the main news crush.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put explicit, headline‑usable material in the first paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Put into the first paragraph something the copy editor can use for headline material: something explicit describing what is happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague puffery in the lede; give concrete facts and figures that make headline writing easy and increase placement chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dredge events for multiple factual angles — 'there's plenty of news'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ample and genuine news lurks in almost any event to be publicized; a publiciteer must dredge for facts to find many story possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take even tame affairs and mine them for multiple stories by digging for facts, processes, outcomes, and human angles.
